note: The plain-English Q&A. Each question sets levers or fields on the nodes the sentence created. 'target' is a node type, 'subjects' (people who aren't staff), or 'flow' (asked once; answers set fields on the flow itself with 'flow'). A question with several matching nodes is asked once per node; {title} is the node's name. 'type' is 'single' (pick one answer) or 'checklist' (tick any that are true; each item has 'on' and 'off' settings). 'show_when' hides a question or item unless it's true. 'skip_when' skips a question we already know the answer to (from the product directory or a company card). The interview also skips any question where no answer would change the result, and records it as assumed, not asked.

questions.why: Each one changes how sensitive the data is, or what the people concerned must be told. Select any that apply.

items.label: It describes how a person is doing
items.hint: Marks, attendance, behaviour, feedback, support notes

items.label: It could reveal health, SEND, religion, ethnicity, sexuality or criminal matters
items.hint: The most sensitive kind of data. It stays in organisation systems or an approved route, and needs an extra legal condition.

items.label: It contains free text or recordings
items.hint: Essays, comment boxes, recordings: the content is unconstrained.

items.label: We already hold it, collected for a different purpose
items.hint: Attendance records kept for registers, now used to predict who may withdraw

items.label: We would be collecting it for the first time
items.hint: A new form, a new login, a new survey

items.label: Under-18s will use the tool themselves
items.hint: A revision app students log into. The ICO's Children's code then applies.

questions.ask: Once in the tool, will {title} identify people by name?
questions.why: Replacing names with a code is often the simplest way to make a proposal easier to approve.
questions.example: A candidate number instead of a name, with the list kept inside the organisation.

answers.label: By a code we can look up

questions.ask: What is the lawful basis for using {title}?
questions.why: Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis. Consent sounds safest, but it is often invalid for students and staff, who cannot freely refuse the organisation.
questions.example: Teaching, marking and supporting students are part of a school or college's job, so 'public task' usually fits.

answers.label: It is part of our public task
It is needed for a contract with them
Consent, and they can refuse with no consequences
Consent, but refusing is not a realistic option
Not sure; refer to the DPO

questions.why: These are the indicators the ICO uses to identify high risk. Selecting one does not mean no; it means a closer look is needed.

items.label: It produces a mark, grade, score or prediction about a person
items.hint: A suggested grade, a risk score, a 'likely to pass' flag

items.label: Outcomes can take effect without a person checking first
items.hint: An automatic fail, an automatic referral

items.label: It could deny someone a service or a right
items.hint: Blocking enrolment, refusing an extension, removing access

items.label: It covers a whole cohort, or more than a thousand people
items.hint: Every student in the college, not one class

items.label: It runs continuously rather than once
items.hint: Weekly checks rather than one survey

items.label: It tracks what individuals do, when or where
items.hint: Login times per student, what they click, where they are

questions.ask: Have the people the data concerns been told about this use?
questions.why: People have a right to be told. Usually this is a paragraph in the privacy notice.
questions.example: A sentence in the student privacy notice about using AI to help with marking.

answers.label: Yes, it is in our privacy notice

questions.why: The same product differs by plan. Free and personal plans usually train on what you enter and come with no contract; business plans do not train and include a data protection agreement.
questions.example: Free ChatGPT on personal logins, versus ChatGPT Business paid for by the organisation.

questions.ask: Two further checks. Does either apply?
questions.why: These are often skipped. If either applies, the design must change before anything else, so it is better to know now.

items.label: We could get the same result with less data, or without names
items.hint: If a less intrusive design achieves the same result, the law expects you to use it.

items.label: We could not show, delete or explain someone's data on request
items.hint: People have these rights whatever the tool.

questions.ask: What will the AI in {title} be used for?
questions.why: Your organisation sets a minimum level of assurance for each kind of AI use. The closer it is to a final decision, the more assurance is needed.
questions.example: Drafting a lesson plan is very different from suggesting a grade.

answers.label: General work with no personal data
Work with things people can be identified from

questions.ask: Will {title} sign a data protection agreement and act only on our instructions?
questions.why: A company that handles your data must be bound by contract. If they will not sign, the answer is no, whatever else is true.
questions.example: Microsoft's Data Protection Addendum covers Microsoft 365 and Copilot.

questions.ask: Could {title} use what you enter to train its AI?
questions.why: If they train on it, the data leaves your control permanently. Free and consumer versions often do.
questions.example: Consumer chatbots often train on chats unless you opt out; business versions usually do not.

answers.label: No, the contract rules it out

questions.ask: Who will own the risk and decide whether to accept it?
questions.why: Someone with the authority to change the project must accept any remaining risk in writing. The DPO advises; they do not approve. A risk nobody owns is the one that goes wrong unnoticed.
questions.example: A deputy principal, or the head of the department running it. A role, not a name.

answers.label: The head of the department running it
